title: RoAR-VAE: Improving Latent Diffusability through Robust Prediction

paper.title: RoAR-VAE: Improving Latent Diffusability through Robust Prediction
paper.abstract:
Abstract An effective visual tokenizer must preserve image fidelity while producing latents that downstream diffusion models can learn efficiently.
Prior work improves latent diffusability through semantic alignment or joint tokenizer–diffusion training.
Revisiting REPA-E, a representative approach, we find that removing its diffusion objective and dedicated generative blocks while retaining semantic prediction from corrupted latents yields comparable downstream generation performance under a matched setting. This observation motivates a general principle of robust prediction : generation-relevant information should remain recoverable from corrupted latents.
We instantiate this principle with two complementary objectives. RobustAlign predicts pretrained semantic features from corrupted latents to preserve high-level structure, while RobustRecon reconstructs the clean image to retain fine-grained spatial and appearance information. Together, they form Ro bust A lignment and R econstruction VAE ( RoAR-VAE ).
Our analysis suggests that robust prediction improves diffusability by making useful information more accessible in high-variance latent directions, which diffusion models tend to learn earlier.
Empirically, RoAR-VAE improves average generation benchmark performance by 2.19 points over the strongest baseline tokenizer under the same training budget, while improving small-text reconstruction accuracy by 16.93 percentage points over FLUX.1-VAE. These results demonstrate that RoAR-VAE achieves a favorable balance between reconstruction fidelity and downstream generative learnability.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Visual tokenizers define the representation on which latent diffusion models learn to generate images ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Esser et al., 2024 ) . An effective tokenizer should preserve sufficient image information for faithful reconstruction, while organizing that information into a representation that a downstream diffusion model can learn efficiently. This latter property, often referred to as diffusability , can conflict with reconstruction fidelity: higher-capacity or weakly regularized latents may retain more visual detail yet be harder to model. Balancing reconstruction quality and diffusability is therefore a central challenge in visual tokenizer design. Recent work improves latent diffusability through semantic supervision during VAE training ( Yao et al., 2025 ; Yao et al., 2026 ) or joint optimization of the tokenizer and diffusion model ( Heek et al., 2026 ; Duggal et al., 2026 ) . A representative approach, REPA-E ( Leng et al., 2025a ) , combines both ideas: as shown in Fig. 2 (a), it jointly trains a VAE and a diffusion Transformer while aligning intermediate features with semantic targets from pretrained visual encoders ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Oquab et al., 2024 ) . However, only the semantic alignment objective directly updates the tokenizer encoder, while gradients from the diffusion objective are detached. This raises a natural question: what actually drives the diffusability improvement in REPA-E, joint diffusion training or semantic supervision? To isolate these factors, we simplify REPA-E by removing the diffusion objective and its dedicated generative blocks while retaining prediction of pretrained visual features from corrupted latents, yielding RobustAlign (Figure 2 (b)). Under a matched evaluation, the resulting tokenizer achieves comparable downstream generation performance to the tokenizer trained with REPA-E (Table 1 ), indicating that noisy semantic prediction alone can provide an effective learning signal for shaping a diffusion-friendly latent space. RobustAlign suggests a broader principle of robust prediction : generation-relevant information should remain predictable from heavily corrupted latents. By backpropagating this prediction objective through the corrupted latent, the tokenizer encoder is encouraged to organize target-relevant information so that it remains accessible under corruption. RobustAlign primarily supervises object-level structure and high-level visual content captured by pretrained features, but may underrepresent fine-grained spatial and appearance variations. We therefore introduce RobustRecon , which applies the same principle to the clean image itself, encouraging detailed image content to remain recoverable from corrupted latents. Combining the two objectives yields Robust Alignment and Reconstruction (RoAR) (Figure 2 (c)). Both auxiliary objectives shape the encoder through corrupted latents, while the standard VAE reconstruction objective preserves faithful reconstruction from clean latents. The latent PCA visualizations in Figure 3 further illustrate their complementary effects: RobustAlign emphasizes object-level organization and foreground–background separation, RobustRecon exposes richer local variation, and their combination exhibits both forms of structure. We further ask: why does robust prediction improve diffusability? Under Gaussian corruption, higher-variance latent directions retain a higher signal-to-noise ratio and are therefore more robust to noise. Training the encoder to recover clean targets from corrupted latents consequently encourages generation-relevant information to remain accessible in these dominant directions, potentially by strengthening the principal modes or by enriching the image information they encode, as suggested by the PCA visualizations in Fig. 3 . Prior analyses further show that higher-variance covariance modes tend to be learned earlier by diffusion models ( Wang and Pehlevan, 2025 ) . Together, these observations suggest that robust prediction organizes useful information into prominent latent structure that can be acquired more readily by a downstream diffusion model. Figure 1: Reconstruction versus generation. RoAR-VAE achieves a favorable trade-off, combining low reconstruction LPIPS with strong diffusability. Empirically, we train RoAR-VAE on ImageNet and evaluate reconstruction and downstream text-to-image generation, using a common diffusion backbone and dataset across tokenizers. RoAR-VAE achieves a favorable balance between reconstruction fidelity and generative learnability (Fig. 1 ): it attains the best performance across three text-to-image benchmarks, with an average score 2.19 points above the strongest included baseline. At the same time, it maintains high-fidelity reconstruction, achieving 32.88 dB PSNR and 0.0349 LPIPS at 256 2 256^{2} resolution, while improving small-text reconstruction accuracy over FLUX.1-VAE by 16.93 percentage points (Table 3 ). Ablations further show that RobustAlign and RobustRecon provide complementary gains, and that latent corruption is critical to downstream performance. These results support robust prediction as an effective principle for improving latent diffusability while retaining high reconstruction fidelity.

sections.heading: Improving diffusability of tokenizers.
sections.text: Latent diffusion separates perceptual compression from generative modeling ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Esser et al., 2024 ) , motivating visual tokenizers that balance reconstruction fidelity with downstream learnability ( Skorokhodov et al., 2025 ; Yue et al., 2026a ) . Pre-trained visual representations ( Oquab et al., 2024 ) have improved latent diffusion through representation alignment in the denoiser ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Singh et al., 2026 ) as well as regularization of the tokenizer ( Leng et al., 2025a ; Yao et al., 2025 ) . Recent work builds tokenizers directly on frozen pre-trained encoders ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) , while subsequent approaches address the loss of fine-grained information when repurposing such encoders for generation ( Chen et al., 2026a ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Yue et al., 2026b ; Shi et al., 2026 ) . A complementary line of work jointly optimizes the tokenizer and diffusion model ( Vahdat et al., 2021 ; Heek et al., 2026 ; Duggal et al., 2026 ; Leng et al., 2025a ) to better align latent representations with generative learning. Other approaches improve tokenizer representations through equivariance and perturbation-based regularization ( Kouzelis et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: Learning dynamics of diffusion models.
sections.text: Training dynamics influence both what diffusion models learn and when. Wang and Pehlevan (2025) derive an inverse-variance learning timescale for tractable denoisers, showing that higher-variance covariance modes are learned earlier. Our work revisits REPA-E ( Leng et al., 2025a ) , a representative approach that combines semantic enhancement with joint tokenizer–diffusion training, and highlights robust prediction as an effective source of supervision for improving latent learnability. The spectral bias of diffusion dynamics offers a complementary explanation: robust prediction makes generation-relevant information more accessible in dominant latent modes, which downstream diffusion models tend to learn earlier. Figure 2: From REPA-E to RoAR. (a) REPA-E jointly trains the tokenizer and diffusion model, but only semantic alignment backpropagates through corrupted latents to the tokenizer encoder. (b) RobustAlign-VAE isolates this semantic-prediction pathway by removing the diffusion objective and its associated modules. (c) RoAR further introduces RobustRecon, combining semantic and image reconstruction targets under latent corruption alongside the standard VAE objective on clean latents.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: Overview. Our goal is to learn a VAE latent space that supports both faithful reconstruction and efficient downstream diffusion learning. We begin by revisiting REPA-E (§ 3.1 ) and isolate the supervision that directly shapes the tokenizer encoder. This leads to RobustAlign (§ 3.2 ), which predicts pretrained semantic features from corrupted latents without jointly training a full diffusion model. We then introduce RobustRecon (§ 3.3 ), which instead reconstructs the clean image from corrupted latents to preserve fine-grained spatial and appearance details that semantic features may underrepresent. Combining the two objectives yields RoAR-VAE . Finally, we discuss a possible explanation for the diffusability gains by making semantic and spatial information more accessible in dominant latent modes (§ 3.4 ).

sections.heading: Simplifying REPA-E.
sections.text: REPA-E improves the VAE while jointly training a diffusion model, even though the flow-matching loss itself does not update the VAE encoder. This joint training requires a full generator and also prevents caching latents for large-scale training. We therefore ask: is the improvement in diffusability driven by joint VAE–diffusion training, or by semantic prediction from corrupted VAE latents? To isolate these factors, we introduce RobustAlign , shown in Figure 2 (b). RobustAlign-VAE removes the flow-matching objective and all network components used only for diffusion prediction, retaining only the standard VAE objective together with semantic prediction from corrupted latents. sections.heading: Representation view.
sections.text: To examine how noisy semantic prediction changes the latent representation, Figure 3 visualizes the leading principal components of the latent space. Compared with the reconstruction-only baseline in Figure 3 (b), RobustAlign in Figure 3 (c) exhibits clearer object-level organization, with more coherent within-object regions and stronger foreground–background separation. This qualitative pattern is consistent with semantic prediction making target-relevant structure more accessible in dominant latent directions.

sections.heading: 3.3 Robust Reconstruction and the RoAR Framework
sections.text: RobustAlign encourages semantically organized latent representations, but semantic targets may underrepresent fine-grained spatial and appearance details that are also important for downstream generation. As illustrated in Fig. 3 (c), RobustAlign produces coherent object-level structure, yet local variations within an object, such as texture and boundaries, are less prominent. This motivates a complementary objective that encourages detailed image information to remain recoverable from corrupted latents.

sections.heading: RobustRecon: Preserving fine-grained details.
sections.text: As shown in Figure 2 (c), RobustRecon introduces an auxiliary decoder G ξ G_{\xi} that predicts the clean image 𝒙 \bm{x} directly from the corrupted latent 𝒛 t \bm{z}_{t} : ℒ RobustRecon ​ ( ϕ , ξ ) = ℒ MAE ​ ( G ξ ​ ( 𝒛 t ​ ( ϕ ) ) , 𝒙 ) + ℒ LPIPS ​ ( G ξ ​ ( 𝒛 t ​ ( ϕ ) ) , 𝒙 ) , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RobustRecon}}(\phi,\xi)=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MAE}}\left(G_{\xi}(\bm{z}_{t}(\phi)),\bm{x}\right)+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LPIPS}}\left(G_{\xi}(\bm{z}_{t}(\phi)),\bm{x}\right), (5) where the two terms measure pixel and perceptual reconstruction error, respectively ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) . G ξ G_{\xi} shares the architecture of the VAE decoder but uses independent parameters and is discarded after tokenizer training. Beyond standard posterior sampling in VAEs ( Kingma and Welling, 2013 ) , RobustRecon applies corruption over a broad range of noise levels, including latents with very low signal-to-noise ratios. The resulting objective backpropagates through 𝒛 t \bm{z}_{t} to the encoder, encouraging fine-grained image information to remain accessible under corruption. As shown in Fig. 3 (d), RobustRecon exposes richer local spatial and appearance variations than RobustAlign, although its object-level foreground–background organization is less pronounced.

sections.heading: Overall framework.
sections.text: RobustAlign encourages noisy latents to preserve high-level semantic structure, whereas RobustRecon encourages them to retain fine-grained image details. We therefore combine the two objectives into RoAR-VAE , short for Ro bust A lignment and R econstruction VAE, as illustrated in Fig. 2 (c): ℒ RoAR = ℒ VAE + λ A ​ ℒ RobustAlign + λ R ​ ℒ RobustRecon , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RoAR}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{VAE}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RobustAlign}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RobustRecon}}, (6) where λ A \lambda_{\mathrm{A}} and λ R \lambda_{\mathrm{R}} balance the two auxiliary objectives. Both objectives supervise the encoder through corrupted latents, but use complementary clean targets: pretrained semantic features for RobustAlign and the original image for RobustRecon. As shown in Figure 3 (e), their combination yields latent representations that retain both coherent object-level organization and richer local structure, including clearer boundaries, textures, and intra-object variations.

sections.heading: Robust prediction promotes key information in dominant modes.
4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: We briefly summarize the training and evaluation setup here; full implementation details are provided in Appendix A . Tokenizer training. RoAR-VAE uses a convolutional architecture ( Esser et al., 2021 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ) with 8 × 8\times spatial downsampling, 32 latent channels, and approximately 84M parameters. For controlled comparison with prior tokenizer studies, we train exclusively on ImageNet ( Deng et al., 2009 ) at 256 2 256^{2} resolution. Training proceeds in two stages: (1) a 200k-step VAE warm-up using ℒ VAE \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{VAE}} , followed by (2) 250k steps of RoAR refinement with λ A = 1.5 \lambda_{A}\!=\!1.5 and λ R = 0.5 \lambda_{R}\!=\!0.5 . For RobustAlign, the semantic predictor F η F_{\eta} comprises an 8-layer Transformer ( Ma et al., 2024 ) followed by an MLP projector. It is trained to predict the output features of a frozen DINOv2-B encoder ( Oquab et al., 2024 ) . For RobustRecon, the pixel predictor G ξ G_{\xi} is initialized from the stage-one VAE decoder D ψ D_{\psi} . The corruption level is sampled uniformly as t ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) t\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1) . Downstream generative modeling. To evaluate latent diffusability, we freeze each tokenizer and train the same text-conditioned diffusion Transformer from scratch on a filtered and recaptioned LAION dataset ( Schuhmann et al., 2022 ) at 256 2 256^{2} resolution. We use an MMDiT backbone ( Esser et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2026b ) with 24 layers, a hidden dimension of 1024, and approximately 0.8B parameters, together with a frozen Qwen3-0.6B text encoder ( Yang et al., 2025 ) . For tokenizers with different downsampling factors, we adjust the patch size to keep the diffusion sequence length fixed. Baselines. We compare against tokenizers from large-scale generative systems, including SD3-VAE ( Esser et al., 2024 ) and FLUX.1-VAE ( Labs, 2024 ) , as well as recent methods targeting improved latent diffusability, including VA-VAE ( Yao et al., 2025 ) , VTP ( Yao et al., 2026 ) , PAE ( Yue et al., 2026b ) , and REPA-E-FLUX ( Leng et al., 2025b ) . We additionally report FLUX.2-VAE ( Labs, 2025 ) as a reference, but exclude it from baseline comparisons because its tokenizer training data and training recipe are undisclosed. Evaluation protocol. For reconstruction, we report rFID, PSNR, LPIPS, and SSIM on the ImageNet validation set at 256 2 256^{2} resolution, and evaluate text and facial detail preservation using TokBench ( Wu et al., 2025 ) . For generation, we train a downstream diffusion model for each tokenizer under the controlled setup above and evaluate on GenEval ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ) , GenEval2 ( Kamath et al., 2025 ) , and DPG-Bench ( Hu et al., 2024 ) . Each score is averaged over four independent sampling seeds, and we report the arithmetic mean across the three benchmarks as a summary metric. sections.heading: 4.2 Main Results
sections.text: Reconstruction versus diffusion learnability. Table 2 compares RoAR-VAE with existing visual tokenizers in terms of reconstruction quality and downstream generation under a fixed 32k-step training budget. RoAR-VAE achieves a favorable balance between the two objectives, substantially improving reconstruction while maintaining strong downstream learnability. Compared with the reconstruction-oriented FLUX.1-VAE, RoAR-VAE improves PSNR by 1.80 dB and reduces LPIPS from 0.0510 to 0.0349, while outperforming the strongest competing learnability-enhanced tokenizer by 2.19 points on the average downstream benchmark score. RoAR-VAE also approaches the reconstruction and generation performance of FLUX.2-VAE, a strong industrial tokenizer with a similarly balanced reconstruction–generation trade-off. Generated image quality. Figure 4 qualitatively compares downstream generation across different tokenizers. RoAR-VAE produces clearer object shapes and finer visual structure, including more distinct animal contours, sharper suitcase and bag textures, and more regular soccer-ball patterns. Compared with the reconstruction-driven FLUX.1-VAE, these results indicate faster acquisition of object appearance and structure under the same downstream training budget. VA-VAE also exhibits strong learnability, but its generations are noticeably smoother and contain fewer details, consistent with its weaker reconstruction performance relative to RoAR-VAE. Fine-grained reconstruction. Table 3 further evaluates preservation of challenging text and facial details. RoAR-VAE achieves the best performance across all reported text and face reconstruction metrics. Despite being trained from scratch solely on ImageNet, it improves small-text accuracy over FLUX.1-VAE by 16.93 percentage points and increases small-face similarity from 0.53 to 0.65. Although VA-VAE, VTP, and PAE achieve competitive generation scores in Table 2 , their weaker text and face reconstruction results reveal a substantial loss of fine-grained information. Figure 5 provides qualitative examples of these differences, highlighting distortions in textual and facial patterns introduced by the compared tokenizers.

Both RobustRecon (❷) and RobustAlign (❸) consistently improve over Vanilla-KL (❶) across all three benchmarks, increasing the average score from 50.50 to 59.38 and 62.49, respectively. Removing latent corruption (❺) substantially degrades the average score from 63.86 to 58.47, highlighting prediction from corrupted latents as a key component of the framework. Figure 6 further compares downstream performance throughout training: RoAR-VAE consistently outperforms either robust prediction objective used alone across different training budgets. sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we present RoAR-VAE, a visual tokenizer built on the principle of robust prediction . By revisiting and simplifying REPA-E, we identify prediction of clean targets from corrupted latents as an effective source of supervision for shaping diffusion-friendly representations. We realize this principle with RobustAlign for semantic structure and RobustRecon for fine-grained spatial and appearance details. Our analysis suggests that robust prediction encourages generation-relevant information to remain accessible in prominent latent modes that are more resistant to corruption and tend to be learned earlier by downstream diffusion models. Empirically, the two objectives provide complementary gains, allowing RoAR-VAE to improve downstream generative learnability while maintaining high-fidelity reconstruction. These results highlight robust prediction as a simple and effective principle for designing visual tokenizers that better balance reconstruction and generation.

sections.text: This work evaluates reconstruction performance on a published image reconstruction benchmark ( Wu et al., 2025 ) that includes human faces. However, the proposed visual tokenizer is a general-purpose information compressor and is neither trained specifically on human-centric datasets nor optimized for human-related attributes. For downstream visual generation systems built upon our tokenizer, we recommend adopting appropriate safeguards, such as watermarking and monitoring mechanisms, to mitigate potential misuse.

sections.heading: A.1 Tokenizer Training
sections.text: RoAR-VAE uses the standard convolutional autoencoder architecture adopted by latent diffusion models ( Esser et al., 2021 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ) , with an 8 × 8\times spatial downsampling factor, 32 latent channels, and approximately 84M parameters. The encoder and decoder each contain four resolution stages with channel widths ( 128,256,512,512 ) (128,256,512,512) and two residual blocks per stage. All tokenizer training is performed on ImageNet ( Deng et al., 2009 ) at 256 × 256 256\times 256 resolution. Training proceeds in two stages. We first warm up the tokenizer for 200k optimization steps using the standard VAE objective ℒ VAE \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{VAE}} . The reconstruction objective uses unit weights for the L1 and LPIPS losses, together with a KL regularization weight of 10 − 6 10^{-6} . Adversarial supervision is provided by a DINOv2-S ( Oquab et al., 2024 ) -based discriminator. We then refine the tokenizer for an additional 250k steps using the RoAR objectives with λ A = 1.5 \lambda_{\mathrm{A}}=1.5 and λ R = 0.5 \lambda_{\mathrm{R}}=0.5 . The corruption level is sampled uniformly as t ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) t\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1) . For RobustAlign, the semantic predictor F η F_{\eta} consists of an 8-layer Transformer ( Ma et al., 2024 ) followed by an MLP projector that matches the dimensionality of the target features. We use features from a frozen DINOv2-B ( Oquab et al., 2024 ) encoder as the semantic prediction target. For RobustRecon, the pixel predictor G ξ G_{\xi} is initialized from the VAE decoder D ψ D_{\psi} obtained after the warm-up stage and predicts the clean image from corrupted latents using L1 and LPIPS losses. The complete RoAR framework is optimized with AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) , using a batch size of 256 and a learning rate of 1 × 10 − 5 1\times 10^{-5} .

sections.heading: A.2 Downstream Generative Modeling
sections.text: For each tokenizer, we freeze its parameters and train a text-conditioned diffusion Transformer from scratch on a filtered and recaptioned version of LAION ( Schuhmann et al., 2022 ) . All downstream models are trained at 256 × 256 256\times 256 resolution with a global batch size of 1,024. The diffusion backbone is an MMDiT ( Esser et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2026b ) with 24 Transformer layers, a hidden dimension of 1,024, 16 attention heads, and approximately 0.8B parameters. Text conditioning is provided by a frozen Qwen3-0.6B encoder ( Yang et al., 2025 ) . Because the compared tokenizers use different spatial compression factors, we adjust the latent patch size to maintain the same sequence length for the diffusion Transformer. Specifically, we use a 1 × 1 1\times 1 latent patch size for tokenizers with a downsampling factor of 16 and a 2 × 2 2\times 2 patch size for tokenizers with a downsampling factor of 8. This keeps the number of latent tokens processed by the downstream model consistent across tokenizer variants. For RoAR-VAE, diffusion timesteps are sampled using shifted logit-normal sampling with exponential shifting and μ = 1.5 \mu=1.5 . For each baseline tokenizer, we use its official or recommended timestep scheduler. All downstream models are optimized with AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) , using β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 , β 2 = 0.999 \beta_{2}=0.999 , a constant learning rate of 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} , and a caption dropout probability of 0.1. At inference time, we use an Euler sampler with 50 sampling steps and a classifier-free guidance weight of 5.0.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: SD3-VAE ( Esser et al., 2024 ) and FLUX.1-VAE ( Labs, 2024 ) serve as reconstruction-oriented baselines from large-scale text-to-image systems. VA-VAE ( Yao et al., 2025 ) directly aligns latent representations with pretrained visual features using a margin-based similarity objective, while VTP ( Yao et al., 2026 ) jointly optimizes reconstruction and visual representation learning. PAE ( Yue et al., 2026b ) builds on pretrained visual encoders and regularizes the latent manifold for improved downstream generation. REPA-E-FLUX ( Leng et al., 2025b ) jointly refines the tokenizer and diffusion model through representation alignment; in our evaluation, we use only the resulting tokenizer and retrain the downstream diffusion model from scratch. We additionally include FLUX.2-VAE ( Labs, 2025 ) as a strong reference, since its tokenizer training data and recipe are undisclosed.

sections.heading: Reconstruction.
sections.text: We evaluate reconstruction on the ImageNet ( Deng et al., 2009 ) validation set at 256 × 256 256\times 256 resolution and report reconstruction FID (rFID), PSNR, LPIPS, and SSIM. To further assess preservation of fine-grained content, we evaluate on TokBench ( Wu et al., 2025 ) , which contains challenging text- and face-centric images. For text reconstruction, TokBench reports exact recognition accuracy (T-ACC) and normalized edit distance (T-NED), with separate metrics for small text instances and all text instances. For face reconstruction, it measures cosine similarity between face-recognition embeddings (F-Sim), likewise reporting both small-face and overall results. These metrics complement standard image-level reconstruction measures by directly evaluating whether tokenizers preserve small, semantically important details.

sections.heading: Text-to-image generation.
sections.text: For each tokenizer, we train a downstream diffusion model following Appendix A.2 . Unless otherwise stated, benchmark results are measured after 32k downstream optimization steps, enabling comparison of latent diffusability under a fixed training budget. We evaluate text–image alignment on three complementary benchmarks. GenEval ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ) evaluates compositional generation involving object co-occurrence, spatial relations, counting, and colors, while GenEval2 ( Kamath et al., 2025 ) extends this setting with broader coverage of visual concepts and higher compositionality. DPG-Bench ( Hu et al., 2024 ) focuses on dense prompts containing multiple objects, detailed attributes, and complex relationships. Each reported score is averaged over four independent sampling seeds. We additionally report the arithmetic mean of the three benchmark scores, denoted Avg. , as a compact summary.

Abstract An effective visual tokenizer must preserve image fidelity while producing latents that downstream diffusion models can learn efficiently. Prior work improves latent diffusability through semantic alignment or joint tokenizer–diffusion training. Revisiting REPA-E, a representative approach, we find that removing its diffusion objective and dedicated generative blocks while retaining semantic prediction from corrupted latents yields comparable downstream generation performance under a matched setting. This observation motivates a general principle of robust prediction : generation-relevant information should remain recoverable from corrupted latents. We instantiate this principle with two complementary objectives. RobustAlign predicts pretrained semantic features from corrupted latents to preserve high-level structure, while RobustRecon reconstructs the clean image to retain fine-grained spatial and appearance information. Together, they form Ro bust A lignment and R econstruction VAE ( RoAR-VAE ). Our analysis suggests that robust prediction improves diffusability by making useful information more accessible in high-variance latent directions, which diffusion models tend to learn earlier. Empirically, RoAR-VAE improves average generation benchmark performance by 2.19 points over the strongest baseline tokenizer under the same training budget, while improving small-text reconstruction accuracy by 16.93 percentage points over FLUX.1-VAE. These results demonstrate that RoAR-VAE achieves a favorable balance between reconstruction fidelity and downstream generative learnability. 1 Introduction Visual tokenizers define the representation on which latent diffusion models learn to generate images ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Esser et al., 2024 ) . An effective tokenizer should preserve sufficient image information for faithful reconstruction, while organizing that information into a representation that a downstream diffusion model can learn efficiently. This latter property, often referred to as diffusability , can conflict with reconstruction fidelity: higher-capacity or weakly regularized latents may retain more visual detail yet be harder to model. Balancing reconstruction quality and diffusability is therefore a central challenge in visual tokenizer design. Recent work improves latent diffusability through semantic supervision during VAE training ( Yao et al., 2025 ; Yao et al., 2026 ) or joint optimization of the tokenizer and diffusion model ( Heek et al., 2026 ; Duggal et al., 2026 ) . A representative approach, REPA-E ( Leng et al., 2025a ) , combines both ideas: as shown in Fig. 2 (a), it jointly trains a VAE and a diffusion Transformer while aligning intermediate features with semantic targets from pretrained visual encoders ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Oquab et al., 2024 ) . However, only the semantic alignment objective directly updates the tokenizer encoder, while gradients from the diffusion objective are detached. This raises a natural question: what actually drives the diffusability improvement in REPA-E, joint diffusion training or semantic supervision? To isolate these factors, we simplify REPA-E by removing the diffusion objective and its dedicated generative blocks while retaining prediction of pretrained visual features from corrupted latents, yielding RobustAlign (Figure 2 (b)). Under a matched evaluation, the resulting tokenizer achieves comparable downstream generation performance to the tokenizer trained with REPA-E (Table 1 ), indicating that noisy semantic prediction alone can provide an effective learning signal for shaping a diffusion-friendly latent space. RobustAlign suggests a broader principle of robust prediction : generation-relevant information should remain predictable from heavily corrupted latents. By backpropagating this prediction objective through the corrupted latent, the tokenizer encoder is encouraged to organize target-relevant information so that it remains accessible under corruption. RobustAlign primarily supervises object-level structure and high-level visual content captured by pretrained features, but may underrepresent fine-grained spatial and appearance variations. We therefore introduce RobustRecon , which applies the same principle to the clean image itself, encouraging detailed image content to remain recoverable from corrupted latents. Combining the two objectives yields Robust Alignment and Reconstruction (RoAR) (Figure 2 (c)). Both auxiliary objectives shape the encoder through corrupted latents, while the standard VAE reconstruction objective preserves faithful reconstruction from clean latents. The latent PCA visualizations in Figure 3 further illustrate their complementary effects: RobustAlign emphasizes object-level organization and foreground–background separation, RobustRecon exposes richer local variation, and their combination exhibits both forms of structure. We further ask: why does robust prediction improve diffusability? Under Gaussian corruption, higher-variance latent directions retain a higher signal-to-noise ratio and are therefore more robust to noise. Training the encoder to recover clean targets from corrupted latents consequently encourages generation-relevant information to remain accessible in these dominant directions, potentially by strengthening the principal modes or by enriching the image information they encode, as suggested by the PCA visualizations in Fig. 3 . Prior analyses further show that higher-variance covariance modes tend to be learned earlier by diffusion models ( Wang and Pehlevan, 2025 ) . Together, these observations suggest that robust prediction organizes useful information into prominent latent structure that can be acquired more readily by a downstream diffusion model. Figure 1: Reconstruction versus generation. RoAR-VAE achieves a favorable trade-off, combining low reconstruction LPIPS with strong diffusability. Empirically, we train RoAR-VAE on ImageNet and evaluate reconstruction and downstream text-to-image generation, using a common diffusion backbone and dataset across tokenizers. RoAR-VAE achieves a favorable balance between reconstruction fidelity and generative learnability (Fig. 1 ): it attains the best performance across three text-to-image benchmarks, with an average score 2.19 points above the strongest included baseline. At the same time, it maintains high-fidelity reconstruction, achieving 32.88 dB PSNR and 0.0349 LPIPS at 256 2 256^{2} resolution, while improving small-text reconstruction accuracy over FLUX.1-VAE by 16.93 percentage points (Table 3 ). Ablations further show that RobustAlign and RobustRecon provide complementary gains, and that latent corruption is critical to downstream performance. These results support robust prediction as an effective principle for improving latent diffusability while retaining high reconstruction fidelity. 2 Related Work Improving diffusability of tokenizers. Latent diffusion separates perceptual compression from generative modeling ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Esser et al., 2024 ) , motivating visual tokenizers that balance reconstruction fidelity with downstream learnability ( Skorokhodov et al., 2025 ; Yue et al., 2026a ) . Pre-trained visual representations ( Oquab et al., 2024 ) have improved latent diffusion through representation alignment in the denoiser ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Singh et al., 2026 ) as well as regularization of the tokenizer ( Leng et al., 2025a ; Yao et al., 2025 ) . Recent work builds tokenizers directly on frozen pre-trained encoders ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) , while subsequent approaches address the loss of fine-grained information when repurposing such encoders for generation ( Chen et al., 2026a ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Yue et al., 2026b ; Shi et al., 2026 ) . A complementary line of work jointly optimizes the tokenizer and diffusion model ( Vahdat et al., 2021 ; Heek et al., 2026 ; Duggal et al., 2026 ; Leng et al., 2025a ) to better align latent representations with generative learning. Other approaches improve tokenizer representations through equivariance and perturbation-based regularization ( Kouzelis et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . Learning dynamics of diffusion models. Training dynamics influence both what diffusion models learn and when. Wang and Pehlevan (2025) derive an inverse-variance learning timescale for tractable denoisers, showing that higher-variance covariance modes are learned earlier. Our work revisits REPA-E ( Leng et al., 2025a ) , a representative approach that combines semantic enhancement with joint tokenizer–diffusion training, and highlights robust prediction as an effective source of supervision for improving latent learnability. Our goal is to learn a VAE latent space that supports both faithful reconstruction and efficient downstream diffusion learning. We begin by revisiting REPA-E (§ 3.1 ) and isolate the supervision that directly shapes the tokenizer encoder. This leads to RobustAlign (§ 3.2 ), which predicts pretrained semantic features from corrupted latents without jointly training a full diffusion model. We then introduce RobustRecon (§ 3.3 ), which instead reconstructs the clean image from corrupted latents to preserve fine-grained spatial and appearance details that semantic features may underrepresent. Combining the two objectives yields RoAR-VAE . Finally, we discuss a possible explanation for the diffusability gains by making semantic and spatial information more accessible in dominant latent modes (§ 3.4 ). 3.1 Preliminaries Visual tokenizer. Tokenizer training. RoAR-VAE uses a convolutional architecture ( Esser et al., 2021 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ) with 8 × 8\times spatial downsampling, 32 latent channels, and approximately 84M parameters. For controlled comparison with prior tokenizer studies, we train exclusively on ImageNet ( Deng et al., 2009 ) at 256 2 256^{2} resolution. Training proceeds in two stages: (1) a 200k-step VAE warm-up using ℒ VAE \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{VAE}} , followed by (2) 250k steps of RoAR refinement with λ A = 1.5 \lambda_{A}\!=\!1.5 and λ R = 0.5 \lambda_{R}\!=\!0.5 . For RobustAlign, the semantic predictor F η F_{\eta} comprises an 8-layer Transformer ( Ma et al., 2024 ) followed by an MLP projector. It is trained to predict the output features of a frozen DINOv2-B encoder ( Oquab et al., 2024 ) . For RobustRecon, the pixel predictor G ξ G_{\xi} is initialized from the stage-one VAE decoder D ψ D_{\psi} . The corruption level is sampled uniformly as t ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) t\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1) . Downstream generative modeling. To evaluate latent diffusability, we freeze each tokenizer and train the same text-conditioned diffusion Transformer from scratch on a filtered and recaptioned LAION dataset ( Schuhmann et al., 2022 ) at 256 2 256^{2} resolution. We use an MMDiT backbone ( Esser et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2026b ) with 24 layers, a hidden dimension of 1024, and approximately 0.8B parameters, together with a frozen Qwen3-0.6B text encoder ( Yang et al., 2025 ) . For tokenizers with different downsampling factors, we adjust the patch size to keep the diffusion sequence length fixed. Baselines. We compare against tokenizers from large-scale generative systems, including SD3-VAE ( Esser et al., 2024 ) and FLUX.1-VAE ( Labs, 2024 ) , as well as recent methods targeting improved latent diffusability, including VA-VAE ( Yao et al., 2025 ) , VTP ( Yao et al., 2026 ) , PAE ( Yue et al., 2026b ) , and REPA-E-FLUX ( Leng et al., 2025b ) . We additionally report FLUX.2-VAE ( Labs, 2025 ) as a reference, but exclude it from baseline comparisons because its tokenizer training data and training recipe are undisclosed. Evaluation protocol. For reconstruction, we report rFID, PSNR, LPIPS, and SSIM on the ImageNet validation set at 256 2 256^{2} resolution, and evaluate text and facial detail preservation using TokBench ( Wu et al., 2025 ) . For generation, we train a downstream diffusion model for each tokenizer under the controlled setup above and evaluate on GenEval ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ) , GenEval2 ( Kamath et al., 2025 ) , and DPG-Bench ( Hu et al., 2024 ) . Table 2 compares RoAR-VAE with existing visual tokenizers in terms of reconstruction quality and downstream generation under a fixed 32k-step training budget. RoAR-VAE achieves a favorable balance between the two objectives, substantially improving reconstruction while maintaining strong downstream learnability. Compared with the reconstruction-oriented FLUX.1-VAE, RoAR-VAE improves PSNR by 1.80 dB and reduces LPIPS from 0.0510 to 0.0349, while outperforming the strongest competing learnability-enhanced tokenizer by 2.19 points on the average downstream benchmark score. RoAR-VAE also approaches the reconstruction and generation performance of FLUX.2-VAE, a strong industrial tokenizer with a similarly balanced reconstruction–generation trade-off. Generated image quality. Figure 4 qualitatively compares downstream generation across different tokenizers. RoAR-VAE produces clearer object shapes and finer visual structure, including more distinct animal contours, sharper suitcase and bag textures, and more regular soccer-ball patterns. Compared with the reconstruction-driven FLUX.1-VAE, these results indicate faster acquisition of object appearance and structure under the same downstream training budget. VA-VAE also exhibits strong learnability, but its generations are noticeably smoother and contain fewer details, consistent with its weaker reconstruction performance relative to RoAR-VAE. RoAR-VAE achieves the best performance across all reported text and face reconstruction metrics. By revisiting and simplifying REPA-E, we identify prediction of clean targets from corrupted latents as an effective source of supervision for shaping diffusion-friendly representations. We realize this principle with RobustAlign for semantic structure and RobustRecon for fine-grained spatial and appearance details. Our analysis suggests that robust prediction encourages generation-relevant information to remain accessible in prominent latent modes that are more resistant to corruption and tend to be learned earlier by downstream diffusion models. Empirically, the two objectives provide complementary gains, allowing RoAR-VAE to improve downstream generative learnability while maintaining high-fidelity reconstruction. These results highlight robust prediction as a simple and effective principle for designing visual tokenizers that better balance reconstruction and generation.
